PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

In this sub-strand you will say the sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ clearly using words about hygiene and sanitation. You will also learn how to listen actively to a speaker, how to interrupt politely, and why we take turns when we talk in interviews and debates.

## Strand 10.0: Hygiene and Sanitation
Sub-strand 10.1.1: Listening and Speaking: Pronunciation and Vocabulary
Suggested lessons: 2

## What this sub-strand covers
• Sounds
• Oral presentations
• Interrupting politely

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 10.0 Hygiene and Sanitation, Sub-strand 10.1.1 Pronunciation and Vocabulary

PAGE 2: Learning outcomes

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) articulate sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ accurately for effective communication
b) interact with a speaker actively during an oral presentation, speech or narration for listening fluency
c) interrupt a speaker appropriately for politeness in conversation
d) use vocabulary related to the theme in a variety of contexts for self- expression
e) promote the importance of turn taking in oral interviews or debates for effective oral communication

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should we listen to others?
2. What do you do when you want to talk and your friend is still talking?

PAGE 3: How we will learn

## Learning experiences
• repeat words with the sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ after the teacher or audio recordings accurately
• tell riddles with words containing the sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ with peers
• interact with a speaker or presenter through verbal and non-verbal cues
• engage the audience when making an oral presentation
• watch a video recorded riddling session or listen to an audio recording
• interview one another on a topical issue
• listen to a poem, a story or a song based on the theme and answer questions orally
• use digital devices to record solo or choral poetry performances

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This competence are developed when the learner says the words correctly and when working with peers.
• Self-efficacy: It is developed when the learner communicates accurately thereby enhancing their confidence.

## Values
• Love: It is nurtured when the learner puts the interest of others before their own interests during collaborative activities.
• Responsibility: This is encouraged as the learner solves the given problems proactively by making oral presentations as assigned.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• The learner’s self-esteem is enhanced as they acquire better self-expression and pronunciation ability through engaging in various activities for interactive listening and turn-taking.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner applies the skills of interactive listening to all learning areas as listening is a key skill for effective learning.

PAGE 4: Lesson 1: Sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ in hygiene words

LESSON 1: SOUNDS /Ɪ/, /Iː/, /S/, /Ʃ/ AND /ƏƱ/ IN HYGIENE WORDS
============================================================

## What you will learn
• Say words with the sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ correctly.
• Tell the difference between pairs such as ship and sheep, sip and ship.
• Use hygiene and sanitation words in sentences.

Curriculum outcomes: a) articulate sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ accurately for effective communication; d) use vocabulary related to the theme in a variety of contexts for self- expression

## Introduction
Say these two words aloud: ship and sheep. They look almost the same, but one is a boat and the other is an animal. If you say the vowel wrongly, your listener hears a different word. Today we practise sounds that change meaning.

PAGE 5: Lesson 1: Sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ in hygiene words — The short sound /ɪ/ and the long sound /iː/

## Notes

### The short sound /ɪ/ and the long sound /iː/
The sound /ɪ/ is short. Your mouth is relaxed and the sound is quick. Words: sit, bin, sink, dish, rinse, lid, fill.

The sound /iː/ is long. Stretch your lips a little, as if smiling, and hold the sound longer. Words: clean, sweep, feet, teeth, meal, sea, disease (the second part).

These pairs differ only in the vowel sound:

- ship – sheep
- sit – seat
- bin – bean
- fill – feel
- live – leave

PAGE 6: Lesson 1: Sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ in hygiene words — The sounds /s/ and /ʃ/

### The sounds /s/ and /ʃ/
For /s/, keep your teeth close together and let air hiss out like a snake: soap, safe, sweep, dust, rinse.

For /ʃ/, push your lips forward and round them a little, like when you tell someone to be quiet: shh. Words: wash, flush, brush, shower, sanitation, infection. Notice that in sanitation and infection the letters ti make the /ʃ/ sound.

Pairs: sip – ship, sell – shell, sea – she, save – shave, sore – shore.

### The sound /əʊ/
This sound glides from one vowel to another. Start with your mouth open in the middle and finish with rounded lips: soap, home, toe, bowl, cold, clothes, no.

PAGE 7: Lesson 1: Sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ in hygiene words — Hygiene and sanitation words

### Hygiene and sanitation words
Hygiene means keeping your body and things around you clean so that you stay healthy. Sanitation means the safe removal of waste such as faeces and refuse, for example by using a clean toilet or latrine. Other words you will use: flush, wipe, scrub, rinse, mop, broom, drainage, infection, diarrhoea, cholera.

- After using the toilet, flush it and wash your hands with soap.
- Dirty water can carry diseases such as cholera and diarrhoea.
- We sweep the classroom with a broom and mop the floor.

PAGE 8: Lesson 1: Sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ in hygiene words — Key words

## Key words
• hygiene — keeping yourself and your surroundings clean to stay healthy
• sanitation — safe ways of getting rid of human waste and rubbish
• rinse — wash something in clean water to remove soap or dirt
• infection — an illness caused when germs get into the body

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which word has the long sound /iː/: sit or seat?

Answer: Seat

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Which word has the sound /ʃ/: sell or shell?

Answer: Shell

## Worked examples

### Example 3
Pick the word with the sound /əʊ/: mop, soap, cup.

Answer: Soap

PAGE 9: Lesson 1: Sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ in hygiene words — Say it and riddle it

## Activity: Say it and riddle it
You will need: Word cards: ship, sheep, sip, soap, sweep, wash, bin, bean, flush, home

1. Listen to your teacher or an audio recording say each word, then repeat it after them.

2. In pairs, one learner says a word from a pair such as sit or seat; the partner points to the card they hear.

3. In groups, tell riddles that use the sounds, for example: I am white and slippery, and I get smaller every time you wash your hands. What am I? (soap)

4. Make one riddle of your own using a word with /ʃ/ or /əʊ/ and tell it to the class.

PAGE 10: Lesson 1: Sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ in hygiene words — Practice

## Practice

1. Sort these words into /ɪ/ and /iː/: bin, clean, dish, sweep, sink, teeth.

2. Underline the letters that make the /ʃ/ sound in: wash, sanitation, brush.

3. Write two words with the sound /əʊ/ that are about cleanliness.

4. Use the word flush in a sentence.

PAGE 11: Lesson 1: Sounds /ɪ/, /iː/, /s/, /ʃ/ and /əʊ/ in hygiene words — Summary

## Answers to practice

1. /ɪ/: bin, dish, sink. /iː/: clean, sweep, teeth.

2. wa(sh), sanita(ti)on, bru(sh)

3. Any two, for example soap, clothes, bowl.

4. Example: Always flush the toilet after using it.

## Summary
• /ɪ/ is short (sit); /iː/ is long (seat).
• /s/ hisses (sip); /ʃ/ is made with rounded lips (ship).
• /əʊ/ glides, as in soap and home.
• Hygiene and sanitation words help us talk about staying clean and healthy.

PAGE 12: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking

LESSON 2: ACTIVE LISTENING, POLITE INTERRUPTING AND TURN TAKING
============================================================

## What you will learn
• Show a speaker that you are listening using words and body language.
• Interrupt a speaker politely.
• Take turns in an interview or debate about hygiene.

Curriculum outcomes: b) interact with a speaker actively during an oral presentation, speech or narration for listening fluency; c) interrupt a speaker appropriately for politeness in conversation; d) use vocabulary related to the theme in a variety of contexts for self- expression; e) promote the importance of turn taking in oral interviews or debates for effective oral communication

## Introduction
Imagine your class is holding a debate on whether every learner should carry a handkerchief to school. If everyone speaks at the same time, nobody hears anything. Good listeners and speakers follow simple rules.

PAGE 13: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking — Listening actively

## Notes

### Listening actively
When someone gives a speech, tells a story or makes a presentation, show that you are following:

- Look at the speaker.
- Nod or smile when you agree or understand.
- Keep your hands and feet still; do not play with things.
- Ask a question or make a short comment when the speaker invites you.

These are verbal cues (words, such as "Yes, I see") and non-verbal cues (actions, such as nodding). They tell the speaker that you care about what they say.

When you are the speaker, engage your audience. Look at them, speak loudly enough, ask them a question, or let them guess the answer to a riddle.

PAGE 14: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking — Interrupting politely

### Interrupting politely
Sometimes you need to speak while someone is still talking, perhaps to ask for something to be repeated. Wait for a short pause, raise your hand if you are in class, then use polite words:

- Excuse me, may I say something?
- Sorry to interrupt, but could you repeat that?
- May I add something, please?

After you speak, say "Thank you. Please go on." Do not shout over the speaker or finish their sentences for them.

PAGE 15: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking — Taking turns

### Taking turns
In an interview, the interviewer asks one question and waits for the full answer before asking the next. In a debate, each speaker is given time and the others listen. Taking turns is important because:

- everyone gets a chance to share ideas;
- we hear every point clearly;
- it shows respect for others.

Here is part of an interview:

Amina: Excuse me, Otieno. May I ask you some questions about keeping clean?
Otieno: Yes, of course.
Amina: When do you wash your hands?
Otieno: I wash them before I eat and after I use the latrine.
Amina: Thank you. Why is that important?
Otieno: Because germs on dirty hands can cause diarrhoea.

PAGE 16: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking — Example 1

## Key words
• interrupt — start speaking while another person is talking
• non-verbal cue — a message sent without words, such as a nod or a smile
• turn taking — speaking one at a time and letting others finish
• debate — a formal discussion where people give different views on a topic

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Your friend is telling a story and you did not hear a word. What do you say?

Answer: Sorry to interrupt, but could you repeat that word, please?

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Name one non-verbal way to show you are listening.

Answer: Nodding, looking at the speaker, or smiling.

PAGE 17: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking — Hygiene interviews

## Activity: Hygiene interviews
You will need: Exercise book, A phone or tablet for recording (if available)

1. In pairs, write three questions to ask about hygiene, for example: How do you keep your classroom clean?

2. Take turns to interview each other. The interviewer waits for each full answer.

3. Once during the interview, the listener interrupts politely to ask for something to be repeated.

4. Listen to a short poem or song about cleanliness read by the teacher and answer questions orally.

5. If a device is available, record your group reciting a short poem about hygiene.

PAGE 18: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking — Answers to practice

## Practice

1. Write two polite phrases you can use to interrupt a speaker.

2. Give two reasons why we take turns in a debate.

3. Complete the sentence: A good listener looks at the speaker and ______.

## Answers to practice

1. For example: Excuse me, may I say something? Sorry to interrupt, but may I ask a question?

2. Everyone gets a chance to speak, and we hear every point clearly (it also shows respect).

3. nods / keeps quiet / asks questions when invited

## Summary
• Show active listening with eye contact, nodding and short comments.
• Interrupt only at a pause, using polite words such as Excuse me.
• Take turns so that every speaker is heard.

PAGE 19: Revision quiz

REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word has the short sound /ɪ/?
   A. sheep
   B. ship
   C. clean
   D. feet

2. Which pair differs only in the sounds /s/ and /ʃ/?
   A. sit – seat
   B. sea – she
   C. bin – bean
   D. soap – home

3. Which word has the sound /əʊ/?
   A. broom
   B. mop
   C. soap
   D. dust

4. Which letters make the /ʃ/ sound in the word sanitation?
   A. sa
   B. ni
   C. ti
   D. on

5. Which of these shows you are listening actively?
   A. Looking out of the window
   B. Nodding at the speaker
   C. Talking to your neighbour
   D. Drawing in your book

6. What is the most polite way to interrupt?
   A. Stop! I want to talk.
   B. Excuse me, may I say something?
   C. You are wrong!
   D. Keep quiet now.

7. When is the best time to interrupt a speaker?
   A. In the middle of a word
   B. During a short pause
   C. While shouting
   D. Never, even in an emergency

8. Complete: After using the toilet, ______ it and wash your hands with soap.
   A. flush
   B. sweep
   C. rinse
   D. dust

9. Which word means keeping yourself and your surroundings clean to stay healthy?
   A. infection
   B. hygiene
   C. drainage
   D. refuse

10. Why do we take turns in an interview?

PAGE 20: Quiz answers

ANSWERS
=======

1. B. ship
   Ship has the short /ɪ/; the others have the long /iː/.

2. B. sea – she
   Sea begins with /s/ and she begins with /ʃ/.

3. C. soap
   Soap has the gliding sound /əʊ/.

4. C. ti
   In words ending in -tion, ti sounds /ʃ/.

5. B. Nodding at the speaker
   Nodding is a non-verbal cue that shows you are following.

6. B. Excuse me, may I say something?
   Excuse me and may I are polite words.

7. B. During a short pause
   Waiting for a pause is polite.

8. A. flush
   We flush a toilet to remove the waste.

9. B. hygiene
   Hygiene is about cleanliness for good health.

10. So that each person can finish speaking and be heard clearly, which shows respect.
   Turn taking lets every speaker be heard.

### Interrupting politely
Sometimes you need to speak while someone is still talking, perhaps to ask for something to be repeated. Wait for a short pause, raise your hand if you are in class, then use polite words:

- Excuse me, may I say something?
- Sorry to interrupt, but could you repeat that?
- May I add something, please?

After you speak, say "Thank you. Please go on." Do not shout over the speaker or finish their sentences for them.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking — Taking turns
studyPages.body:
### Taking turns
In an interview, the interviewer asks one question and waits for the full answer before asking the next. In a debate, each speaker is given time and the others listen. Taking turns is important because:

- everyone gets a chance to share ideas;
- we hear every point clearly;
- it shows respect for others.

Here is part of an interview:

Amina: Excuse me, Otieno. May I ask you some questions about keeping clean?
Otieno: Yes, of course.
Amina: When do you wash your hands?
Otieno: I wash them before I eat and after I use the latrine.
Amina: Thank you. Why is that important?
Otieno: Because germs on dirty hands can cause diarrhoea.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking — Example 1
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• interrupt — start speaking while another person is talking
• non-verbal cue — a message sent without words, such as a nod or a smile
• turn taking — speaking one at a time and letting others finish
• debate — a formal discussion where people give different views on a topic

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Your friend is telling a story and you did not hear a word. What do you say?

Answer: Sorry to interrupt, but could you repeat that word, please?

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Name one non-verbal way to show you are listening.

Answer: Nodding, looking at the speaker, or smiling.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking — Hygiene interviews
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Hygiene interviews
You will need: Exercise book, A phone or tablet for recording (if available)

1. In pairs, write three questions to ask about hygiene, for example: How do you keep your classroom clean?

2. Take turns to interview each other. The interviewer waits for each full answer.

3. Once during the interview, the listener interrupts politely to ask for something to be repeated.

4. Listen to a short poem or song about cleanliness read by the teacher and answer questions orally.

5. If a device is available, record your group reciting a short poem about hygiene.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Active listening, polite interrupting and turn taking — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Write two polite phrases you can use to interrupt a speaker.

2. Give two reasons why we take turns in a debate.

3. Complete the sentence: A good listener looks at the speaker and ______.

## Answers to practice

1. For example: Excuse me, may I say something? Sorry to interrupt, but may I ask a question?

2. Everyone gets a chance to speak, and we hear every point clearly (it also shows respect).

3. nods / keeps quiet / asks questions when invited

## Summary
• Show active listening with eye contact, nodding and short comments.
• Interrupt only at a pause, using polite words such as Excuse me.
• Take turns so that every speaker is heard.

studyPages.title: Revision quiz
studyPages.body:
REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word has the short sound /ɪ/?
   A. sheep
   B. ship
   C. clean
   D. feet

2. Which pair differs only in the sounds /s/ and /ʃ/?
   A. sit – seat
   B. sea – she
   C. bin – bean
   D. soap – home

3. Which word has the sound /əʊ/?
   A. broom
   B. mop
   C. soap
   D. dust

4. Which letters make the /ʃ/ sound in the word sanitation?
   A. sa
   B. ni
   C. ti
   D. on

5. Which of these shows you are listening actively?
   A. Looking out of the window
   B. Nodding at the speaker
   C. Talking to your neighbour
   D. Drawing in your book

6. What is the most polite way to interrupt?
   A. Stop! I want to talk.
   B. Excuse me, may I say something?
   C. You are wrong!
   D. Keep quiet now.

7. When is the best time to interrupt a speaker?
   A. In the middle of a word
   B. During a short pause
   C. While shouting
   D. Never, even in an emergency

8. Complete: After using the toilet, ______ it and wash your hands with soap.
   A. flush
   B. sweep
   C. rinse
   D. dust

9. Which word means keeping yourself and your surroundings clean to stay healthy?
   A. infection
   B. hygiene
   C. drainage
   D. refuse

10. Why do we take turns in an interview?

studyPages.title: Quiz answers
studyPages.body:
ANSWERS
=======

1. B. ship
   Ship has the short /ɪ/; the others have the long /iː/.

2. B. sea – she
   Sea begins with /s/ and she begins with /ʃ/.

3. C. soap
   Soap has the gliding sound /əʊ/.

4. C. ti
   In words ending in -tion, ti sounds /ʃ/.

5. B. Nodding at the speaker
   Nodding is a non-verbal cue that shows you are following.

6. B. Excuse me, may I say something?
   Excuse me and may I are polite words.

7. B. During a short pause
   Waiting for a pause is polite.

8. A. flush
   We flush a toilet to remove the waste.

9. B. hygiene
   Hygiene is about cleanliness for good health.

10. So that each person can finish speaking and be heard clearly, which shows respect.
   Turn taking lets every speaker be heard.
